difficulty.from: question type (inference about evidence); the RC bank has no difficulty field

answer.text: a root carries fungal tissue that may hold the tag itself
answer.line: Much of the tag found in a receiving root sits in hyphae wrapped around and through it: fungal tissue, not plant tissue.

steps: Find the caution: paragraph 11, sentence 1, "a tag in a neighbour is not automatically carbon in a neighbour."
Read the reason in sentence 2: whose tissue holds the tag? Much of it sits in hyphae wrapped around and through the root.
Join it to sentence 3. A stem or leaf has no such wrapping, so a tag there is the stricter test.

choices.text: a root carries fungal tissue that may hold the tag itself
choices.note: Sentence 2: what the instruments detect in a root may be fungal tissue, not plant tissue.

choices.text: the tag breaks down before it can travel up into a shoot
choices.note: Nothing says the tag breaks down. Paragraph 9 says instruments detect it at very low concentrations.

choices.text: the fungus strips the tag out of a root before it is harvested
choices.note: The fungus holds the tag in the root, which inflates the reading. Stripping it out runs the problem the other way.

choices.text: leaves are the only tissue instruments can measure accurately
choices.note: Only tissue goes too far: leaves are the stricter test because no fungus wraps them, not because instruments read nothing else.

choices.text: a root holds far less carbon overall than a leaf holds
choices.note: Root and leaf carbon totals are never compared. And a total would not tell you whose tissue the tag is in.

lockIt: Evidence inferences: ask what else could explain the finding. The stricter test rules that out.

spans.quote: Much of what the instruments detect sits in hyphae wrapped around and threaded through the receiving root, which is fungal tissue, not plant tissue
